title: Lambda vs Kappa Architecture
description: Compare Lambda architecture's batch+speed+serving layers with Kappa's stream-only approach, understand the complexity tax of Lambda, and follow LinkedIn's journey from Lambda to Kappa.

segments.text: Lambda architecture processes data through two parallel paths. The batch layer processes the complete dataset — slow but accurate. The speed layer processes real-time data — fast but approximate. The serving layer merges both views. Nathan Marz proposed this in 2011 to handle both historical reprocessing and real-time queries. LinkedIn, Twitter, and Yahoo all adopted it.

Batch layer: nightly Spark jobs compute accurate aggregates over the complete dataset. Speed layer: Flink or Storm processes the real-time stream since the last batch run. Serving layer: queries hit both and merge — batch results are authoritative, speed results fill the gap. Every time the batch layer runs, it overwrites the speed layer's approximations.

Lambda's complexity tax is brutal. You maintain two codebases — batch and streaming — that must produce the same results. Bug in the batch logic? Fix it in two places. Schema change? Update two pipelines. At LinkedIn, they had teams maintaining duplicate logic in Hadoop MapReduce and Samza. The operational overhead consumed more engineering time than feature development.

Kappa architecture, proposed by Jay Kreps at LinkedIn, uses only the stream layer. Everything is a stream. Historical data? Replay the Kafka log from the beginning. Need to reprocess with new logic? Deploy new consumer, replay the log, cut over when caught up. One codebase, one processing framework, one operational model.

Kappa requires replaying the entire Kafka log for reprocessing. If your log has two years of data at one billion events per day, that's seven hundred thirty billion events to replay. Is this practical? What are the alternatives?
segments.thought_prompt: Is replaying 730 billion events for Kappa reprocessing practical? What optimizations exist?

segments.text: Lambda still makes sense when: batch and real-time logic are fundamentally different — ML model training versus serving. When complete dataset scans are necessary — data quality audits. When stream processing can't handle the required query complexity — multi-way joins over historical windows. The batch layer provides a safety net of correctness.

Kappa wins when: the same logic applies to both real-time and historical processing. When Kafka retention is sufficient for your replay needs — weeks to months. When operational simplicity matters more than batch query flexibility. LinkedIn moved their metrics pipeline from Lambda to Kappa and reduced operational incidents by sixty percent.

LinkedIn's journey: started with Lambda — Hadoop for batch, Samza for stream. Maintaining two codebases for the same metrics was painful. They moved to Kappa using Apache Samza reading from Kafka. Reprocessing uses Kafka's log compaction and long retention. New consumers replay from any offset. Pipeline complexity dropped while data freshness improved from hours to seconds.

The reality is most companies end up with a hybrid. Real-time serving uses Kappa — stream processing writing to a serving store. Batch analytics uses scheduled Spark jobs for complex queries over complete datasets. ML training runs on batch data. The key insight: don't force everything into one architecture. Use each approach where it fits naturally.

You're designing a data platform for an e-commerce company. Requirements: real-time fraud detection, daily revenue reporting, weekly recommendation model training, and ad-hoc analytics. Which architecture — Lambda, Kappa, or hybrid — would you choose and why?
segments.thought_prompt: Lambda, Kappa, or hybrid for: real-time fraud, daily reports, weekly ML training, ad-hoc analytics?

segments.text: Lambda provides accuracy through batch with freshness through streaming, at the cost of dual-maintenance complexity. Kappa simplifies to stream-only with log replay for reprocessing. In practice, most organizations use a pragmatic hybrid. The Staff-level insight: choose based on team size, operational maturity, and whether your real-time and batch logic truly differ.
